utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff concluded last week, she just reached Tab 39. May that, please, go on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While that's being done, I will say that we will conclude the witness today. There will be cross-examination. We will, then, deal with the conduct of the proceedings. The Trial Chamber has something to say on that topic which we will do at the end of the day. We have to finish fairly promptly, because we've got another hearing this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quite understand that. There's one or two things that I want to add to the report that I provided you. We were going to deal with the financial report. We've received extensive series of projections. We can deal with them, of course, today in general, but it may be that we will run out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see what the time is. First we need to conclude the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that has gone on the overhead projector, this occasion then, Mr. Poljanic, you're looking at the original of a document, the English translation of which is on the overhead projector, and it is a document coming from Vice-Admiral Jokic requesting of the operative group command for Dubrovnik region that there be a deblockade of Grujic military building on the Island of Mljet, buildings be handed over on the Peljesac Peninsula, return of military equipment, disarming of civil persons in the Dubrovnik region, extra diction of JNA officers who have not regulated their service within the exchange of prisoners, handing over and disarming of all paramilitary formations as indicated, unconditional surrender of the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, and handing over of complete documentation of Dubrovnik National Defence Council. Were you aware of that document at the time of its production?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you receive it or see it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it on the 12th of October, 1991, in a location called Mocici in Konavle in front of the airport runway, near the beginning or the end, it depends which way you look at it, on the western part of the runway, from Captain Milan Zec, Captain of a naval vessel, Captain Milan Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And a few more words from the pleas about the meeting where you received this document, you told us about the location Mocici. What was the atmosphere of the meeting, who else present?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before, we had a meeting on the Kotor destroyer, that I mentioned in my testimony days ago. And at that meeting, the opposing side insisted that at the next meeting, and that's the one we're talking about today, on the 12th of October, that we also bring a representative of the Croatian army. The next day, that is, on the 12th, we arrived to attend, let us call them negotiations. They were to have been held in Cavtat, however when we got to Cavtat, they told us that the talks would take place in Mocici. We went in a jeep. With me was the president of the executive council of Dubrovnik municipality, Mr. Sikic; a representative of the Croatian army, Dr. Antun Karaman; a member of the negotiating team, Mr. Hrvoje Macan, responsible for communal affairs; and Mr. Miso Mihocevic, who was an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remember, Mr. Poljanic we are very pressed for time today and so we must deal with things in summary. On the other side, who was speaking and what was the atmosphere like very briefly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. On the other side, there was Captain Zec, someone who I think was frigate captain, Mr. Sofronije Jeremic. Then I think he was also a frigate captain, today he is an Admiral Zdravkovic. And I don't remember that there was anyone else representing the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... due to the other on the side during this meeting where this ultimatum was handed over?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They welcomed us in an unbelievable manner for me with at least 100 reservists present, with rifles on the ready. We had the feeling that we would be killed. I don't know what the reasons were, but that is how they welcomed us. However, in the meantime, again I don't know how this came about because this hadn't been agreed, European observers came by and the negotiations which were not real negotiations were conducted. Captain Zec gave me this, which I considered to be an ultimatum. I just looked at it fleetingly, and I said literally: "Captain, this sounds like an ultimatum to me. And I think that we can't accept --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was something said about an incident in Ravno?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in response to this statement of mine, Captain Zec said: "I don't know anything. Yesterday, in the village of Ravno, you killed three of our men, and we are going to act. Literally." My response was: "Captain, the village of Ravno is not in Dubrovnik municipality, nor is it in the Republic of Croatia, nor do I have any idea that there were any conflicts there, nor that anyone was killed on either side. He said: "I don't know anything about that, we are going to act. And the next morning, they entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... just lay that on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is Ravno shown on this copy our Exhibit 326, the place indicated on the yellow sticker we can just see on there. Is that the Ravno you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ravno, there it is, yes. Right here. You can see the word written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So he made this reference to Ravno. What else was said at this meeting where the ultimatum was handed over by Captain Zec of importance, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said after that: "We are going to act." And as I said a moment ago, after that, they entered Cavtat. Immediately we left the negotiations, and they entered Cavtat, and occupied they occupied Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We asked if your negotiators, your side, being to reject the ultimatum, for what reasons. Just give the two or three reasons if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was absolutely unacceptable. It would mean surrendering the whole area which hadn't been occupied yet. The town. And to hand over something that didn't exist, you see. They insisted on the handing over of paramilitary formations which really we did not have. How could we hand over something that we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your fears for the population in the event of surrender were what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were resolute to defend ourselves despite the fact that, in the military sense, we were very weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was Admiral Jokic expressed or known political position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic was a part of that army which had already occupied the whole area of Konavle, the western part of Dubrovnik municipality. So there you are; he was a part of that project.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he express any political views or was he known to have any particular political views? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On every occasion, he expressed such political views. And you will have occasion, if you already haven't received the tapes from those days, and then you will hear from him personally what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And his political views, in a nutshell or in a sentence, were what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was part of the project for the creation of a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move on to what happened after the 12th of October meeting. Did you focus on your duties as mayor, and did you have a negotiating team available to deal with future negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that day, that is, after the 12th of October, 1991, those of us who had been in the negotiating team decided, because of our duties in the town itself, we decided to set up a high-quality team which will continue to negotiate with the enemy side. And we did set up such a team. If you wish, I will name them. In any event, that was the last day when I personally took part in the negotiations with the opposing party; the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give us the names, please, of those in the negotiating team.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Niksa Obuljen, who was my deputy also, deputy town mayor. There was Mr. Djuro Kolic, Mr. Miso Mihocevic, Mr. Hrvoje Macan, and Mr. Ivo Simunovic; five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... were complaints made about the shelling of civilian targets and about the living conditions of those in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Complaints were made after each and every shelling, so there were very many complaints due to the very fact that there was a lot of shelling. The opposing party paid no attention but simply, in accordance with their plan, they continued shelling when they felt it to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what extent must the JNA have been aware of the situation in the town and of the number of people defending it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was aware of each and every detail happening in town. First of all, because they had visual contact with the town; they were only a couple of hundred metres away. Secondly, they were informed. Thirdly, we had a radio station that provided accurate information about everything that was going on, and they certainly listened to it. And furthermore, each time there were negotiations, our side would say what had happened, what they had done. So they were aware of each detail of our tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many defenders were there in the first place within Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, I think I said that at the beginning when General Marinovic, who was then colonel and took over the defence of Dubrovnik, I think there were 59 or 69, something like 60 soldiers. Later on, the number increased, but it never reached the figure of 3 or 7.000 as was mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look next at tab 40, and perhaps please place the original briefly on the overhead projector so those viewing can see what the document is. Then hand the original please to the witness and lay the English on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a document, Mr. Poljanic, dated the 26th of October coming from Lieutenant-General Strugar, headed "Supplement to the Message that is Broadcast on Dubrovnik Radio," addressed to Dubrovnik citizens of all nationalities who wish to be evacuated in the directions of Split, Rijeka, Herceg Novi, and Trebinje. And the proposals for the normalisation of life in Dubrovnik and for ensuring the safety in the city of Dubrovnik are listed: Weapons found to be handed over. JNA and European Community Monitor Mission to control the hand-over. ZNG and Dubrovnik MUP members who didn't regulate their residence status to leave the area. Foreign mercenaries to be handed over to the diplomatic mission. Internal affairs to be restored to their earlier state. Party symbols to be removed from public places. It being said that the JNA should guarantee that its members will respect the complete cease-fire and safety of citizens. JNA armed formations not to enter Dubrovnik. JNA to organise the control of entrances and exits to and from Dubrovnik. And the JNA to enable the appropriate work organisations to provide utilities. And a reply was awaited. Were you aware of that document at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... response to it yourself and the negotiating team in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, this is something we couldn't accept because it would mean surrendering the city, surrendering the men, surrendering the area. Then if we had agreed to this, it would have been over for us. This was just a more detailed ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, then, please, the negotiations of the 5th of December. Were there such negotiations? How many people from Croatia conducted them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the negotiations on the 5th of December were held. On the Croatian side was the then minister Dr. Davorin Rudolf; a second minister, Pero Kriste; Mr. Cifric; and other negotiators. The talks were held. There was a discussion about public utilities so that at least minimum conditions for life could be restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... although my normal practice is to display the original, it's probably better if we hand the original straight to the witness, place the first page of the English version on the overhead projector. I'm not going to go through it; it's available to be read. We'll just see what it is. Mr. Poljanic, is this the agreement that was forged in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can deal with the specific terms of it, if asked. Notwithstanding this cease-fire agreement, was Dubrovnik shelled thereafter and into the autumn and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did the JNA remain in the Dubrovnik region notwithstanding this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The western part of Dubrovnik municipality was left by the JNA on the 27th or the 29th of May. And as for the eastern part, they left on the 22nd of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Briefly, then, can you turn to some public appeals that were recorded about the plight of Dubrovnik. Tab 41, original to the witness, English version on the overhead projector. I'm sorry, this is in English in all forms. This goes from --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the Republic of Croatia, Dubrovnik opstina to heads of state, governments and foreign ministers of the European community. And it there sets out, as of that date, its occupation, its lack of utilities, the failure of the army to withdraw and sets out a protest to the international community, with a request for immediate action. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 42, please. This one, the 28th of November. Perhaps we can place one on the overhead projector so that people can take this one and I'll read it from the projector. Place it there rapidly, thank you. This is a document where it sets out UNESCO observers sent to Yugoslavia to Dubrovnik. Canadian. Then we go down three paragraphs. "Mr. Mayor has made strong appeals to all parties in the conflict to respect the principals enshrined in the conventions for the protection of cultural property." Next paragraph, please move it up a bit. "Mr. Mayor in contact with Mr. Poljanic on a daily basis concerning the situation, although observers will monitor the state of cultural heritage, UNESCO has emphasised that its primary concern is for human suffering, preparing an international campaign." Thank you very much. Does that accord with your recollection of events, Mr. Poljanic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, only there is an error. It wasn't the town mayor who contacted Mr. Poljanic, but Mr. Mayor was a High Representative of UNESCO. So it's not mayor as town mayor, but Mr. Mayor, Federico Mayor, and he contacted me, and everything that is stated is true. I did indeed have many contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will place the next one on the overhead projector, tab 40 -- thank you. Place that on the overhead projector, tab 43. And Tab 43 is in the original, but the English translation is at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the foot of the page if you can just move the page a little bit for me. This is a protest against the absolutely unprovoked strong artillery fire today at 5.50 from the region of wherever it is in Dubrava. Do you remember this complaint being made? It's the 6th of December, 1991, from the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember. It was made relatively early in the morning. I think it was about half past 7.00 or 8.00 while the town was still in a situation when it was possible to write such complaints. But after the 6th of December, the destruction was so vast that it was not possible to write up any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. May I have that back, please. Did the Serbs ever acknowledge culpability for the shelling? Did they ever blame any of parts of their forces at any particular grade for any mistakes that they said had occurred?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that they had ever acknowledged that. But I do know that one of the leading people in the region, three months previously in a newspaper, in a weekly, said that he was very sorry for any of the shells that had missed Dubrovnik as the target. He did that, in fact, three months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other exhibit I better just turn back to very briefly, if I can lay it on the overhead projector, it's Exhibit 338, tab 4, coming up. This is a document dated the 5th of October of 1991 from the government of Serbia in Belgrade. Refers to its session of -- the Republic of Serbia's session held on the 4th of October acquainted with the danger to the civilian population in the city of Dubrovnik. Represents a part of Serbian and Croatian history as well as a monument to the world cultural heritage. And then it says this: "Your decision to install paramilitary units, black legions, and numerous foreign mercenaries in a city of invaluable historical and cultural value and to launch an armed attack on settlements in Herzegovina and Boka Kotorska from this position represents a totally uncivilised, inhumane, and undignified act." Any truth in that paragraph, please, Mr. Poljanic? Was there any truth in that allegation made by the government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single detail is truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the fact that this was written. The contents are not truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move on, then, and I'm very nearly at the conclusion. Mr. Poljanic, did you on the 22nd of December of 1991 go to Washington where you met US Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger to whom photographs of the attack on Dubrovnik was shown. And were you aware that Mr. Eagleburger showed the same photographs later to Borisav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't quite confirm that that was actually on the 22nd of December. I thought about, it and it might have been the 19th of December, but I don't think that is the essential point now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear, and if so, through what channels, what Jovic's response was to the photograph shown to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, and this is what he writes about in his book, he talks -- actually, it was said to be an autobiography, it wasn't an autobiography, it was a book about the events. He recognised in that book and said that not even dust fell upon Dubrovnik and he says that those photographs are a montage, that it is all nonsense, that Dubrovnik is completely intact and not even specks of dust fell upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last exhibit, tab 45, please, it's an English exhibit so place it straight on the overhead projector and I'll read it from there. This Is a document -- just start at the top, please. This is a document from the Crisis Committee of Dubrovnik, and it comes from Admiral Jokic: "... regret for the difficult and unfortunate situation that has been created. This was not our order, neither was it close to my sanity to act like this. General Kadijevic has sent a message to you and the ECMM in Dubrovnik on undertaking an energetic investigation on our responsibility and the guilty ones for this event. At the same time, we expect to find out responsibilities on your side for the sake of a thorough clarification of all circumstances in regard with the events from last night and this morning. General Kadijevic has invited me to Belgrade at 1400, so today I will not be able to continue the negotiations... I suggest the following:" Talks to continue, accept an agreement that fire be ceased, put a boat shuttle between Cavtat and Dubrovnik, control of ships, and so on. What do you say about this document? Do you have any comment on this document? It suggests a breakdown in chain of command and communication I think by the attacking forces, if we look on. Was there any such breakdown?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is a true one, but I don't believe the words in it for the simple reason that on the 6th of December, in the afternoon, I talked to the then Minister of Foreign Affairs of Croatia, Dr. Zvonimir Separovic over the phone, and I told him what the situation was like in town. And quite literally that this would perhaps be our last conversation because we expected that -- to die, all of us thought we would die in the town. The whole town was in flames. I think it was around 3.30 in the afternoon. And Dr. Separovic answered, "Stick it out a little longer. I have just been on the line with Mr. Federico Mayor in Paris." That was the number one man in UNESCO there who told me that he had been given guarantees from the very top echelons of leadership in Belgrade, that everything would be over by 4.00 p.m., that everything would be quiet by 4.00 p.m., and that's what happened. Not a single grenade fell after 4.00 p.m. on that particular day which just shows that it was impossible that Belgrade did not know about it, and not only that but that it could put an end to what was going on, and quite obviously did do so in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did Mr. Mayor explain that he was in contact with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't explain it to me directly because he wasn't able to reach me, but he explained this to Dr. Zvonimir Separovic, the then Foreign Minister of Croatia, and Mr. Separovic relayed that information to me, because he was able to reach me by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poljanic. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider it precisely over the adjournment, but I would think something in the region of two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, you started your testimony by elections when you were elected as mayor of Dubrovnik, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall they were not only local elections, but they were republican elections as well for the Sabor or parliament of Croatia? Do you remember that in that year of 1990, when those elections were held, most of the Serbs or can I say all of Banija, Kordun, Nis and Slavonia and so on and so forth voted in favour of the former League of Communists of Croatia, or rather, Racan's party, and that 21 of them were elected as deputies to the assembly on the ticket of the former League of Communists of Croatia, and the Racan party; that is to say, that most of them voted for the former League of Communists of Croatia. Is that correct? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if that is true, how can you claim in your statement, although I have not been given the statement in Serbian, if truth be told, but what I have received in English, you say that after the fall of the Berlin wall, the Serbs saw their chance, the chance of realising some kind of idea about a Greater Serbia. How can you claim that when we have just taken note of the fact, when we have just taken note of what we said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know full well that this idea to great a Greater Serbia was not born then and there, although we are not dealing with history here, this isn't history, but I can respond to that. That's not when the idea and concept was born. It was born far, far earlier. And with the toppling of socialism or rather communism, as a sort of world system at the time, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, quite obviously, some people created conditions for the implementation of precisely this particular irrational project, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was -- the project never existed, as you know very well yourself, and the thesis and concept of a Greater Serbia at the beginning of the last century already, or rather after the Berlin congress and the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was launched by Austria as a danger that loomed from the Serbs in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This idea was launched before that, and you know that very well yourself, but I don't think we need go into a debate on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have to go into a debate on that point.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that full well, perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that perfectly, whose idea it was and how it was used, et cetera, and so do they, those whose idea it was. Now, you showed us a document here, about the formation -- the idea to form a Dubrovnik republic, the movement to form a Dubrovnik republic. Tell me now, did anybody from Serbia take part in that that you know about? It doesn't matter -- I don't want you to say something that you assume, just what you know, on the basis of what you yourself know, did anybody from Serbia take part in that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any direct contacts between anybody in Serbia with somebody from that - what shall we call it? - movement or council to restore the Dubrovnik republic. But there was some sort of logic in it all. Of course, we cannot judge on the basis of assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, I'm just reading what it says here, and here it says movement for whatever it says. That's why I used the word "movement." Otherwise, it does say here: Demilitarised -- that's what it says in the Croatian version, of course, the Serbo-Croatian or Croatian Serbian version, or what is now the Croatian language, that's what it says: A new, modern, demilitarised and democratised democratic republic under the protection of neighbouring republics and the United Nations. So that means under the protection of the United Nations and neighbouring republics. And as you know, Serbia is not a neighbouring republic when we are talking about Dubrovnik. And as you know, it is quite a long way from Dubrovnik anyway. And do you really see any links between Serbia with the events that took place in Dubrovnik, Mr. Poljanic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, no, but it would have been, and you know that very well yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Poljanic. We'll get to that. We'll get to the facts that you have testified about in due course. But what we're saying is that, according to your knowledge, nobody in Serbia did. Now, did you have any meetings with respect to all these events that took place in Dubrovnik with any representative of Serbia at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although high-ranking officials from Serbia did stroll around Dubrovnik at the time I was mayor or president of the municipality, and during your -- during the testimony of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Mesic, you yourself said when he noted that many came to Knin and the surrounding parts, and you said at the time, well, it was enough that they called upon local municipal representatives. Well, those representatives did not call on me. And you were amongst them, you were one of them in my day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you know - and if you don't know - for more than ten years, I spent my holidays in those parts, and when I was vacationing with my family without having any other business to attend to, I really didn't feel duty bound to report to the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to have a meeting with you. It was just proper to do so because I do know, by the way, that you met with other people who suited you. But let's not waste time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. Poljanic, I did like having my holidays in Dubrovnik, as you know. And this is common knowledge. During the events when the first news of them reached me, I was in The Hague at the time. Tudjman was there, Lord Carrington was there too, and I condemned any violence -- any and all violence in the area of Dubrovnik. Now, then, Serbia, the leadership of Serbia, and I personally -- or rather, do you have any knowledge at all about any links that we had to any of those events in Dubrovnik? Do you know about any of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that enough has been said on the subject and talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you say, you talk about the fact that the JNA attacked Dubrovnik, and then you say that the JNA occupied the territories and so on and so forth. I don't want to repeat what you said, not to waste time, but all the events that you talk about date back to 1991, don't they? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. I talk about some in 1992, and a few days ago, up to 1995. The last shell from Trebinje fell in 1995 and killed three innocent people on the beach, young people on the beach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the events that are the main object and subject of your testimony. Now, whether somebody shot a grenade, a shell from somewhere in 1995 from Trebinje or wherever, I don't want to delve into that, but are you conscious of the fact that at that time - and we're talking about 1991 - the SFRY was still in existence and that the Yugoslav People's Army was deployed in the territory of Yugoslavia, that is to say, on its own territory, at the time when all these events that you describe were going on; in September and in October, November, December 1991? So all these dramatic events and all the drama that you have described, this took place on its own territory.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that on the 21st of June, Croatia proclaimed its independence, and this was not contrary to the constitution that you yourself are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Poljanic, if you're asking me that question - although it is my role to ask the questions here and not you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to put some order into this. Mr. Poljanic, could you concentrate, please, on just answering the questions. And both of you, could you remember that what you say has to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be interpreted. So would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer. On the 25th of June, Croatia proclaimed its independence, and according to our concepts and pursuant to the constitution of that state, of the country you're talking about - Yugoslavia - we were free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you happen to read, because you say that everything was done in a constitutional way, this violent secession on the part of Croatia, that it was done in a constitutional way, have you perhaps read the book or what was written about it by the former president of this illegal Tribunal, Mr. Cassese, where it says that you did not have any legal grounds for secession, for breaking away, and that you did that through force of violence. Do you happen to have read that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through this with the previous witness. We have ruled that it is irrelevant as far as the witness is concerned. He is merely giving his evidence of what happened, and what he says is that Croatia was independent. Now, if a point turns on it, a legal point, in due course we will determine where the truth lies and where the law was. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you explained, that it was sometime around the 1st of October that everything started, that the shooting started --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that. Somewhere around the 15th of September, in fact. On the town itself, it was the 1st of October, but otherwise, before. In Konavle, in the Konavle region, it started earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wrote down your words, what you said, so that's what I'm referring to. I'm not investigating the exact details. But Mr. Poljanic, what I want to ask you is this: I have here before me observations and conclusions by the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro. And let me look at the date. It was the 8th of October, 1991. It was an Assembly session. Now, are you aware of the fact that on the 1st of October, there was a commemorative meeting for the entire leadership over there because of the death and killing of a young man who was stationed at the border between Montenegro and Croatia, and who was killed precisely by the forces that were located in the Dubrovnik region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say on the border, on the frontier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the border, under fire from your side. And they were killed by the forces who were located precisely in your area.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee and can sign that that is not true. I guarantee and I sign what I guarantee that not a single Serb or anybody else on the territory of Montenegro on the 1st of October was killed from the Croatian side. Not a single one. I guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of October was when the commemorative session was held.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means they were killed previously, and what you're saying is a lie, a sheer lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the documents that are presented here, they testify to the facts otherwise, but we'll come to you, to what you say. And they go on to say - is this a lie too? - "The war being waged on the border belt between the Republic of Montenegro with the Republic of Croatia has been imposed on the Yugoslav People's Army by the Republic of Croatia. The war is proof and evidence that the threats made by the Croatian leadership and territorial pretensions that they have towards the Bay of Kotor and other areas in the Republic of Montenegro were not empty threats. The border of the Republic of Montenegro with the Republic of Croatia has been jeopardised and is under threat by the aggression of Ustasha formations on the part of the Croatian Republic." Is that incorrect too?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is so incorrect that I didn't expect you to present such incorrect information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, would you remember this is not a matter for debate. You are in a Court. Just answer the questions. They may seem provocative, but just answer them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have read out is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, I am reading the conclusions of the Assembly of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says they are not true. They may be the conclusions, as described. He says they are not true. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is not true regarding territorial pretensions, you know nothing about territorial pretensions in those days that were discussed, of Croatia towards Boka Kotorska, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on? Nothing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the Lipan charter, the June charter, have you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say in it? The Croatian territory includes the Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Bay of Kotor, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow that there may have been some exaggerations, but real pretensions never existed nor are there any now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do allow that there may have been some pretensions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say pretensions; I said inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Is this true, at least: Montenegro does not have an army of its own? I assume you will agree with that. But military conscripts of this republic, on the basis of federal regulations which Montenegro continues to observe, which is an expression of its pro-Yugoslav orientation and determination to defend Yugoslav institutions is taking part in combat operations of the JNA against Ustasha military forces whereby the dilemma as to whether Montenegro is at war or not is nonsense. Montenegro sees Yugoslavia as a state community and any changes in this country have to be made by peaceful means, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Dubrovnik municipality, there were absolutely no Ustasha forces. As to what was going on in Montenegro, that's their problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only saying --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please confirm the fact that there were many accusations against Montenegrins that they did something, and they are saying that they don't have their own army, and that their reservists took part in the JNA as they respect Yugoslavia and Yugoslav institutions. I assume you're aware of that. And that they, of course, advocate a peaceful solution and not violence. Since you say that there were certain clumsiness, there was some clumsiness in expression, on the other hand, Mr. Poljanic, did Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia later on ever express territorial pretensions towards any part outside its own territory? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely aware of that because -- let us talk about the south of Croatia. Because the war in the south of Croatia was waged exclusively because of territorial pretensions towards Croatia. And participating in that war were the Serbian and Montenegrin army. Now, whether you're going to call it a Yugoslav army, that depends on an agreement. These were Serbian and Montenegrin soldiers, and I saw them with my own eyes. They had their guns pointed at me, a hundred of them or so, at those let us call them negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since they were armed and in uniform, if you knew that they were Serbs and Montenegrins, how could you tell? There may have been a Macedonian, a Bulgarian, a Croat, a Hungarian, Romanian, Ruthenian, a Muslim, and there were many of them, of all nationalities, in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with all kinds of insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had the JNA or some other army there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they were wearing all kinds of insignia. They were wearing JNA uniforms with various insignias. There were five-cornered stars and cockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: JNA uniforms had no cockades.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Poljanic. I cannot put to you what you saw.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I am claiming that they didn't have. You explained here that the pretension was to occupy Dubrovnik, then you mentioned Split, Sibenik, Zadar, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Poljanic, after all, our memories are still fresh, and there are documents to confirm this; wasn't the situation quite the opposite? Wasn't it true that in cities all over Croatia, barracks of the JNA were blocked, electricity was cut off, water, and supplies, and fire opened at JNA barracks? Do you remember, for example, we heard here a telephone conversation between the then federal Secretary of National Defence, Veljko Kadijevic, and the late president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, in which Kadijevic requests that the agreement signed with Lord Carrington in Igalo be observed, and placed particular emphasis on the fact that on that day there were very exceptionally strong attacks on the barracks in Sibenik, that this should be stopped, that the army be allowed to withdraw from there. Do you remember these attacks on barracks? Wasn't that true? It wasn't the army attacking Sibenik or Zadar but on the contrary; the barracks were blocked and attacks launched against the barracks and members of the JNA not only in Sibenik and Zadar, but all over Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying is not true, or partially true. There were blockades. But the question is what preceded that. You know very well that the weapons of the Territorial Defence had been pulled out by you from Croatia; and when Croatia was attacked, we had to find a way of getting hold of some weapons. As a result, there were some blockades. But we didn't attack Sibenik, you attacked it, not because of the blockade. We didn't attack Split, you attacked it, and again, not because of the blockade. We didn't attack Zadar but you did, and not because of the blockade. You attacked it exclusively because you needed that territory. And there was no other reason. At the head of that project were you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Poljanic. Your comments are your affair. But you know that this was a conflict between your paramilitary forces and the legal Yugoslav army and its units and its garrisons all over Croatia. So you consider that not to be true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't a conflict between our paramilitary forces and your units. It was not a civil war. It was a pure aggression against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could the JNA commit aggression on territory where it had been present for the past 50 years?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the 25th of June again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, as far as I understand it, you're a diplomat, are you not? You have served in a number of countries, and I assume that you are familiar with some elementary norms. You know when Croatia was recognised by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was partially recognised already on the 15th of January, 1992, and then it went on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we know how things developed. You remember that Germany's recognition was described by Lord Carrington as the death toll for the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who made what judgement I don't know, but what is important is that Croatia started to be recognised then. And it wasn't just 12 countries but more that recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Croatia committed an armed secession from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about, an armed secession?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to those blockades of JNA barracks. You don't know that this happened. You're not aware of that, all over Croatia, of killings and attacks on JNA garrisons? All this is a pure fabrication?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know also about the month of May in Plitvice, May 1991. I know about Borovo Selo, too. I know about Vukovar, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Other people have testified about those things, so we don't have time now to delve into that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're talking about the period after that, and I'm talking about the period prior to that, about the causes and the effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Poljanic. I saw here that you issued a proclamation to citizens. Units of the JNA are in your town for 20 days already, a proclamation to the citizens of Cavtat in which it is said: "We were taught --" "You have been taught from a long period that we are occupiers, and we are not occupiers." The appeal for cooperation, for refraining from attacks against the army, et cetera. Does this -- is this evidence of goodwill and good faith?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is evidence of perfidiousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. You mentioned when speaking about these attacks, their strength and so on, you said that the Yugoslav People's Army was one of the most powerful armies in Europe. I don't know which in order, but you pointed this out, this aspect of the matter.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, you had no defences.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it sensible, then, to say if such a power had intended to capture Dubrovnik, why didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a debatable question to this day. There are many answers to it, to the question why. One of them is that, after all, it would have lost so many men that it couldn't probably justify it, shall we say, in this case, before Montenegro. Secondly, it is a fact that you needed Dubrovnik empty or relatively empty. You know very well that Dubrovnik and Konavle are ethnically almost entirely pure. Why would you need Dubrovnik with an 88 per cent population of Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely you're not --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did you chase out 35.000 Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes, go on. No, Mr. Milosevic, come on. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who chased out 35.000 Croats from Dubrovnik? Did I do that or somebody from the leadership of Dubrovnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must be allowed to finish. Now, just pause a moment for the interpreters. Now, you were answering the question when you were interrupted. Now, if there's anything else you want to add to the question, which was why didn't they take Dubrovnik, if you want to add anything to what you've said already, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've answered that question. I can go on, but I think I've said what is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, when you say because of our or my shells, Serbia is too far away. Perhaps you saw an army that came specially outside the JNA from Serbia to attack Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There are many documents showing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That people same from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them three days ago and I also saw them those days in Dubrovnik when the Yugo army, as you called it, left the area. Those documents are filed here in Court. I saw them last week when I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not calling it the Yugo army, but the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever you liked to call it in 1991. They, they even signed their names, many of them, and they said which units they came from and where they were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You mean members of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, from the territory of Serbia, but they came from all over Yugoslavia, but you just asked me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you both to point out what the interpreters are raising, quite fairly. They are saying could you kindly pause between question and answer. So, Mr. Poljanic, I know the temptation -- you speak the same language, therefore the temptation is to respond immediately to the question. But would you pause. Mr. Milosevic, the same to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to be quite truthful, we're speaking two languages. Mr. Poljanic speaks Croatian and I speak Serbian and by some wonder we understand one another. We understand one another because we lived together for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did it occur to you that since the JNA was such a major power, that it didn't capture Dubrovnik, that it had no intention of capturing it. Did such a possibility occur to you? It had no intention of taking Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were just shown a document of the command of the operative groups signed by Miodrag Jokic. And you called it an ultimatum whereas it says here "to hand over and disarm all paramilitary formations, the so-called National Guards Corps and MUP units to be reduced to the level of the -- of what it was in January 1991." And it is emphasised the first agreement when the Republic of Croatia - that is, Tudjman - had signed that it would do that. Didn't they ask you to do what Tudjman had agreed on and signed in January 1991, to disband the National Guards Corps and to reduce the police to peacetime strength?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the relevant document, which is tab 40 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's just looked at it, and what it says isn't being challenged. It says the disarming of civilians in the Dubrovnik region, handing over the former officers of the JNA with whom relations have not been regulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: My mistake, it's 39, in fact, is the relevant document. The witness should have it in front of him before he's asked the question. Now what -- the witness has the document. What is the question, Mr. Milosevic, about it? What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider it to be a criminal act of some kind the fact that the army is asking for these facilities - I'm going to skip over this - that those facilities should be left - that is such a notorious fact - and then the return of equipment to recruits who had received them, and the disarmament of civilians, which means the disarmament of paramilitary units and formations which were a jeopardy to security in the area. And the disarmament of paramilitary units pursuant to an agreement that Tudjman signed. He said he would put it into effect on the 21st of January, 1991. What is there that the army is calling for and which it did not have complete legal rights to ask of you, and what kind of criminal act did it perpetrate by doing so?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question, but let me repeat. This -- in Dubrovnik, there were no paramilitary formations whatsoever. What did exist was the legal army, and your army even recognised that army because a day before this document, it asked us to bring in the representatives of the Croatian army to negotiations of this date. And we legally sent a representative of the Croatian army to the negotiations on the next day, which was the 12th of October. And he was Antun Karaman, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't know that it was a legal army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why they wrote this and then called the legal army to attend?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they wrote this as an alibi for further attacks. They knew that we had no paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, to what you had and what you didn't have. You said how you were received at the negotiations with Jokic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was with Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, with Zec.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was with Jokic one day prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have jotted down that you said with Jokic on the 11th of October.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to enumerate, among other things, that there was an interpreter there too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not because of our two languages, but because of the blue helmet observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, that's what I wanted to establish. So what you were saying a moment ago, that the observers fell from the sky suddenly appearing there, otherwise you would have been killed, well, those observers I assume, Mr. Poljanic, and I hope you're not going to challenge, that they were there with the authorisation of the Yugoslav authorities and the Yugoslav People's Army, and they were moving around in this zone, in a zone of which the army had control. Is that something you're disputing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm allowing for that possibility, too, but I'm claiming that we didn't know that they would arrive. They suddenly appeared there, how I don't know. I said that a moment ago, and I am saying that here today, I have been saying it three times now. And it's a good thing that they did turn up. Let's make that understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they had a ready interpreter because they did not expect the observers to turn up?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came much later, but let's leave that to one side for now. We've been through that several times. We can go through it again if you have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I have been allotted very little time to put my questions to you, so I'm going to try and focus on as much -- and cover as much ground as possible. You said that the people in Dubrovnik were very happy to see the changes that had taken place from a communist country into a free country. That change.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that Yugoslavia before that was a country that was not free?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you say, that a certain number of Serbs took part in the formation of a branch of the Serb Democratic Party, which advocated a very nationalistic programme and line, how do you bring this into connection with what you said and what we observed before, that most of the Serbs voted in favour of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because we were a truly a democratic authority. We had even forgotten that fact, although at the meeting, you know this very well, there were some very malicious comments and even more malicious songs about the one about Sloban the Salor [phoen], to the verses of that song.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that song?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it goes: "Come on Slobo, send us some salad. We're going to have some meat, so we'll need the salad for the meat. We're going to slaughter the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that song?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a song that was widely sung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were so democratically disposed that the president of the SDS, we took for a time to go to the negotiations with us with the opposite side, to take part in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking myself why not, that's what we did do. Later on for well-known reasons all that fell through. And I consider I have been extensive enough on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you consider that the HDZ programme of 1989 and then 1990 was not a nationalistic one?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, it was sufficiently national, and I would say that it was an okay programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, as you at the time were either already elected or, at any rate, you delved in politics prior to the elections --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I spent quite a lot of time in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But were slogans written out around Dubrovnik that "the Serbs and dogs have no place here, we'll throw you into the pits again," and slogans similar to those?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs start to leave Dubrovnik during that period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know this: According to a report by Amnesty International, I have it here, relating to Veljko Zecevic, and yourself mentioned Veljko Zecevic as well as Aco Apolonije and Milenko Reljic, they were all people from Dubrovnik. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are they Serbs or are the Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Zecevic is a neighbour of mine. Our houses are 20 metres apart. He was an intellectual. For a long time he was president of the Court. He is an elderly man today. We have had proper relations at a point in time. It is true he was -- a lawsuit was brought against him for something, but he was not found not guilty [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a report by Amnesty International which states, and this was during your time, that he was arrested because of accusations that he had founded an independent Yugoslav Democratic Party. A Yugoslav party I emphasise?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, during my time, he was not arrested. I don't want to claim this with great certainty. I know that he was arrested in Zagreb. Exactly when I don't know. But let me say he was -- the charges were lifted against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And 12 other people from Dubrovnik of Serb or Montenegrin, as it says, Serbian or Montenegrin ethnic origin from Dubrovnik. You've also heard about Jovan Pejovic and Milenko Reljic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This one is a little older because when this was written --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reljic is older, and he has been a well-known lawyer, Dubrovnik lawyer for many years. Where he is now, I don't know. But I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in the same Amnesty International report, Milenko Reljic was accused by the Croatian authorities with Veljko Zecevic and another lawyer, Jovan Pejovic who was even arrested by the Croatian authorities, so that they were accused?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Pejovic, I don't know. I know that Reljic very well. Now, what Amnesty International says I can't day, but I do know actually Reljic was not arrested. He was never taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: It says here actually that 12 of them were arrested.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Reljic was ever in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says the accused Pejovic, Milenko Reljic, and so on. But let's not go into that now. Was there any reason? Were they militant Serbs or anything like that, this Reljic, this Pejovic and this Zecevic man? The ones you know, I'm not asking you about the others whom you don't know. But the people you know, was there any reason for them to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again, I don't know and I could even state that he was never arrested, Reljic, but I couldn't actually sign my name to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zecevic, that's true, he was arrested but he was set free. And I've already said that for the third or fourth time. As for this man Pejovic, I don't know who he was. I have no idea who this man Pejovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind, it's not important. But what you're saying is you don't consider that there was any reason for those people to have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't consider that there was reason. And if you want, I can each add that I had heard that Mr. Zecevic had not very nice things to say about the authorities that were in power then from 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a lovely time in prison, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all this took place later on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was arrested in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually it says here in December 1992, he was accused. I think he was arrested later on, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here in this Amnesty International report.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that took place quite a while later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, it says: "On 12 December 1992 Velimir Zecevic was indicted together with 12 other men of Serbian or Montenegrin ethnic origin from Dubrovnik. [In English] Two of his co-defendants, Jovan Pejovic (age 37) and Milenko Reljic (age 70) are lawyers." And then it goes on to say, The defendant currently under arrest and will almost certainly be the only defendant to be present at the trial. [Interpretation] And the rest had allegedly escaped. So that man was in prison at that time, and he was accused on the 12th of December, so he had been in prison from before that time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there's an error there. I think that that happened -- he ended up in prison much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now within this entire context or complex of questions, what measures, in your opinion, when the HDZ came into power and began the persecution of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ did not begin to persecute the Serbs in Dubrovnik. That is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say it began in Dubrovnik; it began in other places in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. But were the Serbs discriminated against in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they dismissed from the police force, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why? Isn't that aggressive behaviour towards them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not discrimination. Everybody was retained, just those who did not want to put on Croatian uniforms were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So they were dismissed, but you just say for that particular reason. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, how many houses, Serb houses in Dubrovnik, were demolished?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've already discussed that. We discussed it last week. You accused me - not you, but your authorities and the papers wrote about - it accused me of having personally - I think the Politika newspaper wrote about it on its title page or on page 2 - that Poljanic had destroyed 400 Serb house in Dubrovnik. That is just one of the lies that were bandied about. Those houses, 400 were not demolished. They were not all residences. When we arrived in 1990, we inherited 7.000 facilities and buildings that were built without authorisation. There were pigeon coops and different kinds of buildings, but there were residential buildings among them, too. I think some 60 facilities, ranging from chicken coops to residential buildings, that were destroyed and demolished, those which could not be incorporated and legalised on the basis of any criteria. When we had used up all the legal means at our disposal to protect them, those were the ones that were demolished. But they were not Serb houses; they were both Croatian and Muslim and Serb homes and houses. That is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Poljanic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. There you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I asked you was whether the houses were destroyed, and you're claiming that they were not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have been told you is the truth. They were, but in the manner in which I have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. What the witness has said is that houses were destroyed, but it was not for any discriminatory reason but because they were built against the regulations. That's what he said. He's said that before, and he's repeated it today. Now, if you've got some evidence to the contrary, you can call it, Mr. Milosevic, but there's no point arguing about it. Mr. Poljanic, help us with this, if you would: An Amnesty report has been put to you in which it appears to say that 12 Serbs or Montenegrins from Dubrovnik were arrested by the authorities in December 1992. And I think you agree that they shouldn't have been, but you only in fact knew about the details of one of them. That is as I understood your evidence and what was put to you. But can you help us about this: What do you know about this case generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can almost claim that 12 of them were not arrested. I know that several -- well, actually, now I know just about Mr. Velimir Zecevic. And let me say again that he was my neighbour and for a long period of time president of the Court. He really was arrested, and he was acquitted, the accusations were withdrawn. Some of them were accused but not arrested, some of them were tried in absentia. But generally speaking about that case, all I can say is, and what I know about it is -- and I don't think it was in 1992. I think it was later. I don't remember the exact date, so let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have before you the Amnesty International report.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But they were people who at that time were accused of having collaborated with the other side. Now, how far they were guilty, I can't say. In the case of Mr. Zecevic, quite obviously there was no guilt because he was acquitted. The charges were withdrawn. So that's the only one I can speak about. I don't even know some of the others. For example, I don't know who this man Jovo Popovic is. Milenko Reljic I do know. I know that he's not in Dubrovnik. I don't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, let's not waste time and let's move on, if possible. You state in your statement that the JNA shot around --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please. I took my earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here, under inverted commas, that you saw that the JNA shot its own villages in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Herzegovina, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean targeted its own villages? What does that mean "its own villages"? What do you mean by saying its own villages, the JNA? What villages did the JNA have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, then this is what it is all about: Before the beginning of the war, that is to say, at the start of July -- September, the army that you're talking about, the JNA, if we're going to agree that that's what its name was, de facto shot at Montenegrin villages, it shot also at the villages in the Konavle region, but then it put out information in the public that it didn't do any shooting. Now, we didn't have anybody to do any shooting there. And they said loud and clear over the radio, in the papers that the Croatian mercenaries, Kurds, Ustashas, and all the terms you used to refer to us were shooting with the intent of taking control of the Bay of Boka. And in that way, you managed to recruit a lot of people in Montenegro who later on marched on Dubrovnik. And I state once again, and I claim, and I can sign my name to that, that not a single bullet was shot from Konavle into Montenegro. Quite literally not a single bullet from a revolver, let alone a mortar, a gun cannon or whatever they're called, these military devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poljanic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are at the time we should adjourn. But before we do, Mr. Milosevic, do you want that Amnesty report exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, you can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have the report, please. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not in relation to this, only when you're about to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll exhibit that. We'll have a number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to do with the evidence of this witness. It's clear that we won't reach discussions about procedural matters until the third session of the morning. There are some additional documents that I hope will be of considerable value to the Chamber that I would be distributing then. As you're going to have two short breaks between now and then, I propose to distribute two of them now. They are documents you have seen before in an earlier form. We call them fill-box documents. They are documents that record the evidence in a systematic way. There's one for Kosovo which is in a file, one for Croatia thus far which is in a clip like this. If I can distribute them now, they may be of value because you'll have a chance, however brief, to review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, as far as I understand it, you're claiming something rather unbelievable, and that is that the JNA was opening fire and killing in the territory of Montenegro. So those eight men killed at the border crossing for whom a commemoration was given on the 1st of October in Montenegro were not killed by your forces, but by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said. If there were men killed, then I claim that they were killed on the territory of Croatia by the army of Serbia or Montenegro. So it wasn't a case of our men opening fire and killing them on the Montenegrin side. I never said that. What I was saying was that our people never fired a single bullet across the border to Montenegro.
