utterances.text: As you can see, the whole of the old city is in one piece, and I know that it was your members of the National Guard which set fire to the library of the Serbian orthodox church which, as you see, was the only seriously damaged facility in the old town. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. That is not at all the building of the library of the Serbian orthodox church. This is the building of Ivo Grbic a Dubrovnik painter, the house he lived in all his life, and from which he carried out his old mother on his hands who was 90 years old. And this inscription, icons --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Icons, that's fine there was a shop of icons, but it is written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Cyrillic. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that indicate the origin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you see nobody destroyed those inscriptions indicating where the icons were. But this building is not the building of the Serbian library, but rather the building owned by Ivo Grbic that I went to hundreds of times and which was razed to the ground. That's one point. This may be the best photograph of all that I have seen. I think that quality is very bad and very little can be seen, probably, for technical reasons. So I don't see how anyone could see anything. One could just see a little piece of what was destroyed on the fence of the St. Vlaho Church, the patron saint of Dubrovnik. By then the town had been cleaned up. It was a notorious fact that 1.500 shells fell on the town. That on the main street, Stradun, 56 shells fell. It is also a notorious fact that the Franciscan monastery received 53 hits. It is also a notorious fact that the Dominican monastery, which was also shown here, was hit by 23 shells. It is also a fact that the St. Vlaho, who was shown here, also received five shells. And this Tribunal will receive the documents about this when the next witness comes, who is an architect and director of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments and who is an expert in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness, help us with this: The accused has suggested that the orthodox library was burned down by members of the ZNG. Can you help us with that, first of all, whether the library was burned down, and secondly whether -- if it was, whether it was done by members of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guarantee, with everyone that it is possible to provide guarantees with, that there were no, no attacks by members of Zengas, which is in fact the National Guards Corps, were carried out against the library of the orthodox church. Everything that was damaged in Dubrovnik, including that library, if it was damaged - to tell you the truth, I don't know that it was, but if it was, I accept it - was the result of the shelling of this army that we have well agreed to call it the Serbian/Montenegrin, or Yugoslav. Whichever you like. I guarantee it was by them. Not a single other shell was not fired at Dubrovnik by anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you have listed a number of the buildings. How come they didn't fall down after these numerous shells that you have listed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well how Dubrovnik was built. You know perfectly well that buildings which lean on one another, it is very difficult to demolish, even with shells. But almost each was hit, almost each, not each and every one, with one or more shells. All the roofs were destroyed, so when you approach Dubrovnik from the highway, from the hill, you no longer see the roofs with patina who developed this patinated colour of the centuries. You see new red-tiled roofs because each and every roof had to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, commenting on the first tape, you said it was taken before. But that on the 23rd and the 24th of October, the old city was shelled.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said two shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that after that, there was more shelling, even though the old city was demilitarised, as you say, and there was no action from it. How, then, do you explain that on the 30th of October, 1991, a week later, a week after the date you mention as the shelling -- date of the shelling of the city, so it is the last day in the month of October, the 30th of October, foreign diplomats, including the ambassadors of Great Britain, the Netherlands, Italy, and Greece, and the deputy ambassador of the United States of America, toured the city and establish that the old city had not been damaged except for a few buildings on the edges which were insignificantly damaged without any proof as to who had provoked the damage, and that these stories of about 15.000 shells or however many you mentioned have absolutely no foundation. An official announcement was issued that all of us were able to hear in the media on the 30th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I have told the truth. If I am mistaken, then I may be mistaken by saying a small number. The truth is that on the 12th of October, I said that at least 15.000 shells fell on Dubrovnik. If I erred, I erred by reducing the number, not by increasingly. Not only did the diplomats come, but the Libertas convoy arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but these people came and we all heard their announcement.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way that those other 30 or so -- I beg your pardon. In the same way that the 30 journalists that I received and who, after the surroundings of Dubrovnik had been bombed, except the old city, they came to the old city, filmed it, saw that it wasn't damaged, and that information was sent to the world. But not the surroundings of the old town. They were not allowed to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, you just said that they saw that the old city was not damaged. And you said that 15.000 shells fell on the old city?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. God forbid, I never said on the old city. I said 1.056 on the old city. But on Dubrovnik as a whole, more than 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 1.056 shells fell, and it wasn't damaged --

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they fell afterwards. Up to that date, that is, the 23rd of October, there were only two shells. One on Boskovic Street, the one going up hill to towards Buzi, as you know well, and the other, the roof of the Rupe museum. If somebody doesn't want to see it. They need not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this map or sketch marked by witness Stipan Jelavic where you can see the positions from which fire was opened at the JNA. Is it then at least clear that the JNA was only responding to fire coming from these positions firing at it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not clear, nor can it be clear. The JNA was attacking Dubrovnik and it was under no circumstances responding to fire coming from Dubrovnik as there was no such fire. The positions that he marked here, all of them, with the exception of -- in fact, there's not a single position in the old town. On this sketch, I don't see a single position in the old city. I don't see it. Not a single one. Not even on this sketch that you have shown me, and with the word "Jelavic" on it. I don't see a single position in the old city which is fully in accord with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that the army invaded, attacked, its own territory, because after all Yugoslavia still existed in those days, and the army was responding to fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have put point this frequently, and the witness has dealt with it. Now, unless you have something new, we must bring this to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Fine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if the Court will grant us time, I realise we're in a difficult position today, it being the end of the term so to speak, but there is five minutes that I would like to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the first of the videos that Mr. Milosevic showed you this morning, it was clear, from what you said, that a number of journalists had been invited to Dubrovnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that time, who was in effective control of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Dubrovnik was controlled by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say "us," you mean a Crisis Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who ran the police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the defence of Dubrovnik, who was running that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the end of September onwards, then Lieutenant-Colonel at the time, or rather, Colonel and today General Nojko Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, my questions are only directed from the 1st of October until the end of December.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Marinovic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In inviting those journalists on that occasion, did you invite other journalists and film crews on other occasions to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't invite those journalists. Let's clear that point up. Those journalists arrived, they turned up. To be quite frank, I don't know how they came there, got to be there. We didn't invite them. And after that, we did invite a lot but it was so difficult to reach Dubrovnik that many of them didn't come. But those who did arrive, I must say, sent out very proper reporting, proper reports out to the world. But there were those who filmed this kind of stuff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What one of those journalists appeared to be saying was that there was provocation taking place by people within Dubrovnik firing at the Serbs, expecting a retaliation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody said that, they were telling lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I want to put to you is this: Was what you were undertaking during the period of October until the end of December a publicity campaign within Dubrovnik in an attempt to turn world opinion against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you mean -- I don't know what you're referring to when you say what we did. Could you be a little clearer, please. "What you were undertaking," you said. Now what did that refer to? Do you mean the information that we sent out to the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, were tyres being burned in the streets to give an impression of bombs having been, or shells having been fired, and that the city was on fire? Were tyres lit in the streets to give an impression of fire?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a heinous lie. I swear that they were not. The tyres were burning from the burnt cars which the Yugo army set fire to on the parking lot. So the cars burnt down and so did the tyres, and anything else that could be put alight. But no Croatian or Croatian soldier set fire to a single tyre to create smoke and send out information to the world that Dubrovnik was alight. Now, we must agree upon this; Dubrovnik was alight, it had suffered worse than ever in its history and that so many shells were thrown on Dubrovnik that were thrown. Let's accept that truth and agree to that because it is the truth which has been documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were gun positions put on the top of buildings so that shots could be fired at the JNA to enable a retaliation that you knew would occur?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that question isn't clear to me. There were no nests or guns on any roofs. I'm not -- I don't understand your question. Would you repeat it, please. Which roofs do you mean? The tops of which buildings? What tops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You heard the journalists describe a man on top of the hotel firing with a machine-gun, and the journalist saying what was going to be expected was that there was going to be firing back. Was that deliberately being done to provoke a reaction?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What reaction? Why would we do that? To provoke somebody to shell us back? Where's the logic there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, as a policy to get a condemnation of the Serbs, using Dubrovnik as a well-known place.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything we did, all the information we sent into the world, we did exclusively in order to protect the town and the area around Dubrovnik, or rather, the Dubrovnik municipality, which was as it was then. And for no other reason whatsoever. Just in order and exclusively to have the world learn about the truth. We knew that Dubrovnik was a very important town. It was a world cultural heritage site. And the information that we sent out into the world we sent exclusively for the purpose of protecting ourselves. There were no other reasons at all; for the world to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It has been suggested to you or at least inquired of you whether you were drawing fire down onto yourself and onto your ancient city. Any truth in that, and has that ever been suggested to you before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was put forward all the time. At that time, nobody -- let me tell you the people of Dubrovnik loved their town too much to allow themselves to fire a single shot at their own town. This is really beyond all belief. So nobody, none of the inhabitants of Dubrovnik, no -- or people living in the surrounding parts ever fired a single shot at Dubrovnik. Not only in this war, but either previously or afterwards. And for the men of Dubrovnik, the town of Dubrovnik is sacred. And it is the only town which is written when it is says city, the word "city" is written in capital letters, or "town."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The suggestion that Serbs were persecuted in some way for this war, any suggestion that the Serbs of Dubrovnik were subject to reduction of privilege or in any other way persecuted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No rights were taken away from them, nor were they persecuted in any way. Let me say, we have been here for such a long time and this was not mentioned at all: There were Serbs from Dubrovnik even who, very honourably, joined the ranks of the Croatian army and together, with all the rest, defended Dubrovnik. And there are some of them from the area who are in the Croatian army to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused asked you a question in slightly different terms about any links that there may have been between the attack on Dubrovnik and Serbia itself. And you said that enough had been said about those links to Serbia. Tell us, please, but only by title or topic, what events, what features of this history link these events, not just to the JNA but to Serbia itself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, there is exclusively one link for everything that has happened. One link. And that is the attempt to form a Greater Serbia. Nothing else than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was suggested, I think, that the JNA was composed of all ethnicities. What do you say about that at the time with which we are concerned in Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the JNA at that time, the Slovenes had left, and so had the Croats and the Macedonians. They had all left the JNA by that time, and largely even the Albanians. They had already left. And as for the claim that several Croats had also been killed in the Dubrovnik area on the Yugoslav army side, that is true. They were the Croats who, from Montenegro, they were citizens of Montenegro and they were in the army, in the Yugo army. And of course, quite obviously and naturally, they were among the occupying forces and I'm sure that in some of the fighting, some of them had probably been killed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying with Montenegro and returning to the topic of arguable links to Serbia, are you yourself of any apology that has been made publicly by the president of Montenegro, now the Prime Minister, Mr. Djukanovic, for events that happened in your city?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. President Djukanovic did apologise to the Croatian people for what had happened in South Croatia in which the citizens of Montenegro had taken part. I must also state one more thing here, with respect to that topic: In the course of the war, at Cetinje - and Cetinje is a Montenegrin town, very old and ancient, at one time the capital of Montenegro - the liberals organised a rally, a meeting, at which at that time there were a lot of people, 200.000 people, in fact. It was no easy matter to gather together such a large number of people. And they sang from Mount Lovcen that the fairy is saying forgive us Dubrovnik, the verses of the song to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware - just yes or no, and if you can't remember, don't say so - but are you aware of whether in his apology, Mr. Djukanovic made any reference to Serbia? If you're not aware and can't remember it, we'll probably be able to play the tape of the apology in due course, but can you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that particular detail, but you can play the tape and I'll be able to tell you after I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not now, another time, I think, for want of time. Are you aware also of Serbs in Serbia itself demonstrating in favour of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit 328, Tab 8. We don't have time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubrovnik, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serbs in Serbia protesting in favour of the suffering in Dubrovnik, a rally held in Belgrade on the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I did hear that there were individual sorts of protests, but not a mass rally of that kind. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, a matter of detail about one of those two films. The film that showed, you said, Ivo Grbic's house razed to the ground, how was it razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR POLJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not razed to the ground. The walls remained standing because the walls are linked to the neighbouring houses, adjacent houses. But it burned down to the ground. And this happened exclusively as the result of the shelling. It received several shell shots, and of course, quite normally, one of them set fire to the wooden construction, whether between the storeys or the roof construction, but it did burn down to the ground, and the walls remained standing. It has been reconstructed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give you. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are proposing, in fact, to adjourn at half past, because we have another hearing in an hour's time. It may be helpful if we could briefly hear from the amicus on the Jelavic statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I've given some thought to this, Your Honours, because it seems essential that there needs to be some sort of control and a test of relevancy rather than increasing documentation unnecessarily. If the accused produces a statement in cross-examination and a witness adopts the passage that is being put, then quite clearly, that passage is able to be put into evidence and the document should be marked in some way to denote the relevant passage and that it is entered into the proceedings through that way. If the Prosecution then go on to cross-examine in relation to the same document, and the witness adopts further passages, then that further material should also be likewise identified to show what has been brought into evidence. The practice of putting the whole document in, in my submission, produces more extraneous and irrelevant material that shouldn't really be before the Trial Chamber because it has not been dealt with explicitly. If a passage is also put into cross-examination from a statement produced by the accused, and the accused agrees that the Trial Chamber, for sake of convenience should have a copy of the document so that they can see what is being put and understand it perhaps more clearly, then such a document becomes an aid, and that should only be marked for identification purposes. And then at a later stage, in our submission, the Trial Chamber or the accused himself may call the witness and have the document produced, if need be, through direct evidence. It seems that that's, in our submission, the fairest way of dealing with material because we can have a problem of if one side wants statements produced, the other side wants statements produced, that we're not really going to be sure what we're dealing with in terms of evidence in the trial from the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is yet another suggestion, if I may say so, which we'll have to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we can resolve this at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness adopts the passage, and if the Prosecution doesn't oppose to admit the witness statement, is there any obstacle to admit such a document, especially if it is a statement given to an OTP investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a fifth category Your Honour has pointed out, and I would agree that if a waiver has taken place, and obviously if it's an OTP document, they will have considered the matter themselves from their own perspective, and be prepared to waive an objection in those circumstances. But it's an issue whether there is objection to the content or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other issue is the sheer amount of material which we may be accumulating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would caution against any practice that starts admitting little bits and pieces of statements. I think your general rule has been out-of-court statements can form the subject matter of questions if the question is acknowledged. Then the answer of the witness is evidence in the case, and you don't need the trigger question to identify what it is he's saying to be produced as an exhibit. And my only concern this morning was, as it has been on several occasions, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ensure that questions are asked in a fair context. Making an exception for a particular statement was an exception, and keen though I am to have a much larger documentary base in the form of witness statements, generally another argument possibly for another day, possibly never to be raised again, I respectfully suggest that it's better to stick to your normal policy and to make this an exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you accept in this particular case the Jelavic statement it should go in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy for it to go in, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But in the light of the absence of objection, the Jelavic statement will be admitted. This is not to be seen as any precedent for future rulings. Now, Mr. Nice, we have literally a minute left. There's a matter I want to deal with myself about the future conduct, briefly. It' really by way of stating what our current conclusions are. If there's anything urgent you'd like to raise, of course you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I've supplied you with a confidential document which might have merited or benefitted from a short, and indeed confidential, discussion because the purpose of its being confidential is set out in its last or second to last paragraph. I was hoping just to amplify the purpose and to explain a couple of rather, I hope, helpful things, encouraging things, but I would rather do it confidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Given the time, I wonder if you could do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because I don't think it will affect what we're going to say. Time is against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If by chance, it might affect what you're going to say I must, of course, ask for liberty to come back on it. But I hope that you'll accept, and this is really fundamental to the submissions that we have made to you in writing, I hope you'll accept that our intention is to achieve exactly the general result that we know the Chamber wants in terms of brevity and to do it in a way that meets everybody's requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will -- I have been passed a note about the exhibits. The statement will be Exhibit D74. We'll consider whether to admit the two videotapes, which would be 75 and 76. But we will leave that decision. It may be that the one without sound could be admitted, since it's a factual one apart from the various comments on it. The other one is in a more controversial position and I would have thought probably should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then Your Honours. Perhaps one thing I can say publicly is that the two documents I provided you with this morning, the one about Kosovo and the one about Croatia, are documents I have forecast right from the beginning of this trial I would be providing, and the one about Croatia and the one about Bosnia, that is also in a state of preparation, are documents that I will be preparing in any event. But if they serve a useful purpose, and I think they can serve a very useful purpose in control of the trial, I will do my best, by allocating resources, to have them prepared on a regular basis so that you will never be very far out of date with the use that this document can make for you and indeed for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll resolve the question about the videos by simply marking both for identification, 75 and 76. We've received a number of reports recently, including a medical report on the accused. We've received submissions from the parties. So it's right that the parties should know what the proposal, the thinking of the Trial Chamber is as to the conduct, the future conduct of the proceedings, since it affects them. And in summary form, our conclusions are these: One, the trial will proceed according to timetable, due allowance being made for illness and such rest days as appropriate. There will be no other extension of time for the Prosecution case. Two, Defence counsel will not be imposed upon the accused against his wishes in the present circumstances. It is not normally appropriate in adversarial proceedings such as these. The Trial Chamber will keep the position under review. Three, as we have previously ruled, the accused will not be provisionally released, as he has asked, during the course of these proceedings. The case is now adjourned until the 9th of January. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
